hook: Stephen Cole Kleene was born on January 5, 1909, in Hartford, Connecticut, and graduated summa cum laude from Amherst College in 1930 before earning his doctorate at Princeton University in 1934 under Alonzo Church. At Princeton he helped develop the theory of computable functions, and in 1936 he published General Recursive Functions of Natural Numbers, proving the equivalence of Church's lambda calculus, Godel's recursive functions and other formal notions of computability. He spent most of his career at the University of Wisconsin, where he became the Cyrus C. MacDuffee Professor of Mathematics and Computer Sciences and served as dean of the College of Letters and Science from 1969 to 1974. In a 1951 RAND Corporation report published in 1956 as Representation of Events in Nerve Nets and Finite Automata, he introduced what he called regular events, the notation now known as regular expressions, to describe the behavior of McCulloch-Pitts neural nets in formal, searchable terms. Kleene was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1969, received the National Medal of Science in 1990, and died on January 25, 1994.

quick_facts: Born January 5, 1909, in Hartford, Connecticut, and died January 25, 1994.
Graduated summa cum laude from Amherst College in 1930 and earned his Princeton doctorate in 1934 under Alonzo Church.
Helped prove the equivalence of lambda-definability, general recursiveness and Turing computability, formal ideas now grouped under the Church-Turing thesis.
Introduced regular events, the basis of regular expressions, in a 1951 RAND report published in 1956 as Representation of Events in Nerve Nets and Finite Automata.
Spent most of his career at the University of Wisconsin, where he became the Cyrus C. MacDuffee Professor of Mathematics and Computer Sciences.
Elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1969 and awarded the National Medal of Science in 1990.

achievements.title: General Recursive Functions of Natural Numbers (1936)
achievements.impact: Helped establish the equivalence of the major formal definitions of computability, a foundation for computer science and the theoretical study of what algorithms can do.

achievements.title: Regular expressions (1951/1956)
achievements.impact: Gave computing a compact notation for describing patterns in sequences, now used throughout programming languages, search tools and text-processing systems.

achievements.title: Kleene's recursion theorem
achievements.impact: Provided a foundational result in recursion theory describing self-referential computable functions, later applied to programs that can refer to their own code.

achievements.title: Introduction to Metamathematics (1952)
achievements.impact: Became a standard textbook that trained generations of logicians and computer scientists in recursion theory and formal logic.
